snippet.title: Did people eat spoiled meat in the Middle Ages?
snippet.description:
There is a common myth (repeated even in classrooms) that Europeans in the Middle Ages wanted spices from Asia to cover up the taste of spoiled meat. What the heck? Who eats spoiled meat? Medieval Europeans were no more capable of or willing to eat rotten meat than any other human beings.

I also mention in this video some of the ways medieval Europeans preserved meat without electrical refrigeration.

Check out the Crash Course World History playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLBDA2E52FB1EF80C9

snippet.title: How do snakes swallow animals so much bigger than they are? - Niko Zlotnik
snippet.description:
Explore how snakes evolved, and find out how their jaw-dropping anatomy allows them to take down prey several times their size.

--

Since slithering onto the scene some 150 million years ago, evolving length and limbless-ness out of their ancestral lizard forms, snakes have diversified rapidly. Their noodly bodies and flexible heads granted them access to novel places and prey. And today, there are nearly 4,000 snake species, spanning habitats high and low. Niko Zlotnik explores how snakes evolved into incredible predators.

Lesson by Niko Zlotnik, directed by Anna Benner.

snippet.title: Medieval Arabic names had 5 parts, but no surname
snippet.description:
There have been many systems for naming people over the centuries, but English-speakers tend to be familiar only with their own system. While it is true that modern Western surnames evolved in medieval Europe, there were other even more complex naming systems in use in other parts of the world prior to that.

In this video we take a look at the naming system used among Arabic speakers in the Islamic Middle East prior to modern times.


CORRECTIONS

1. I messed up the Arabic on the Spongebob slide. I didn't use the right grammatical form for the word "minutes." That's pretty embarrassing, honestly. In my defense, the Arabic rules for number agreement are out of control. (Needless to say, I'm not fluent in Arabic. This is not news to any Arabic speakers watching the video.)

2. The English word "camel" doesn't come from Egyptian Arabic. It comes from Phoenician by way of Greek. Phoenician and Arabic are both Semitic languages. In most Semitic languages the word for "camel" is some variation of "gamal," "gamla," etc.

3. I didn't talk about how kunyas can also be laqabs. Not so much a mistake as an omission. When I made the video I just didn't want to add extra explanation when it was already pretty long. But in retrospect, after seeing some of the comments, I see that I was leaving out an important and interesting part of Arabic naming.

snippet.title: The Untold Daily Life of Anglo-Saxon Families (950 AD)
snippet.description:
In this video, we travel back to the ultimate turning point in British history—the exact decade that forged the nation of England. Following the dramatic defeat of the fierce Viking warlord Eric Bloodaxe, the Anglo-Saxons finally united. But surviving in this raw, unpolished world was an intense daily struggle.

We’re taking you off the muck-filled streets and stepping right through the heavy timber doors of a real Anglo-Saxon home. Discover the intense reality of daily medieval survival: from breathing thick wood smoke and sharing your bedroom with livestock to keep from freezing, to eating endless pots of boiling pottage. But it wasn't all misery! We also explore how these resilient people blew off steam with brutal wrestling matches, complex strategic board games, and epic storytelling around the hearth fire.

Experience the raw, unfiltered truth of early medieval life—mud, mead, and all!

snippet.title: Why does the Electoral College exist?
snippet.description:
Forget what you think you know about why they created the Electoral College.


0:00 Background
1:14 The Constitutional Convention of 1787
2:24 Direct election of the president?
6:58 Congressional appointment of the president?
11:11 Congressional apportionment bonuses
14:55 The logic of an electoral college
20:38 Why the small states and slave states were skeptical of an electoral college
21:50 The Brearly Committee
22:35 Let's read the Constitution
31:50 The president's term of office and re-electibility
33:49 What would you have done?
34:57 Footnotes


FOOTNOTES

The primary source used for this video is The Records of the Federal Convention of 1787, ed. Max Farrand, rev. ed., 3 vols. (New Haven, Conn.: Yale University Press, 1966 [1911, 1937]). It collates the notes taken by different individuals regarding the debates and votes at the convention sequentially according to date. I cite the dates below.

[1] Wilson and Morris’s advocacy for direct election of the president and the arguments made against it by other delegates: June 1, July 17, July 19

[2] Gerry’s concern about an interstate political organization: July 25

[3] See the credentials of Delaware’s delegates in Appendix B of The Records of the Federal Convention of 1787, vol. 3, pp. 574–575. See also James Madison’s notes on the debate on May 30 (vol. 1, p. 37).

[4] Debates on whether states should have equal or proportional representation in Congress: May 30, June 9, June 11, June 19, June 27–30, July 7

[5] Wilson and Morris’s advocacy of an electoral college: June 2, July 19, September 4. Other delegates also sometimes spoke in favor.

[6] Shlomo Slonim, “The Electoral College at Philadelphia: The Evolution of an Ad Hoc Congress for the  Selection of a President,” The Journal of American History 73, no. 1 (June 1986), 55–56.

[7] Wilson proposed that electors be proportional to population: June 2

[8] Ellsworth proposed a 3-2-1 scheme: July 19

[9] The delegates did approve an electoral college on July 19 and then reverted to selection by Congress on July 24. During those days the draft had the electors being chosen by state legislatures, with the largest states getting three electors and the smallest getting one. They did not switch back to an electoral college until September.

[10] The Brearley Committee's solution to have electors vote within their respective states: September 4. Madison recorded the rationale, as expressed by Gouverneur Morris, in vol. 2, p. 500.

[11] Houston’s concern over the distance electors would have to travel: July 24. Hugh Williamson of North Carolina had also voiced this concern on June 2.

[12] Morris voiced this view on July 17 (vol. 2, p. 33)

snippet.title: The haunting history of the Paris Catacombs - Stephanie H. Smith
snippet.description:
Take a tour of the vast, underground network of the Paris Catacombs, and find out how this 18th century cemetery came to be.

--

For centuries, Parisians had buried their dead in the Cemetery of the Innocents. By the 18th century, the grounds had become overcrowded — spewing foul odors across the city. Residents worried that it posed a public health threat, and petitioned the government for a solution. But where could they move millions of remains? Stephanie H. Smith explores the vast, underground network of the Catacombs.

snippet.title: Why Most Medieval People Didn’t Know Their Own Age...
snippet.description:

In the Middle Ages, most European Medievals lived a rural life, a life that used the rising and setting of the sun, the changing seasons, the ebb and flow of the tides and the movements of the moon and stars to dictate their actions and choices. The clergy and monks lived their lives to the extremely rigid routine of a finely honed, liturgical calendar of devotional days and daily, timed prayers, all the while accompanied by the use of sundials, water clocks, astrolabes and eventually mechanical clocks.  

Let’s travel back in time to the Middle Ages and take a look at why it is so difficult to know what day it was, why there were three dates to celebrate the New Year and why there were no minutes.

snippet.title: How Birmingham Evolved From Medieval Cesspits to Modern Showers & Toilets (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
This is the real, untold story of how Birmingham fought disease, poverty, and its own filth across nine centuries to become the city it is today (1100s-2000s). Featuring the River Rea, the back-to-back slums, Joseph Chamberlain's water revolution, and the extraordinary 73-mile Elan Valley pipeline that changed everything.

Lessons Learned from this video:
1) Population growth without infrastructure planning is a death sentence, not just an inconvenience
2) One determined mayor with a public health vision saved more Birmingham lives than any doctor of his era
3) A city's greatest invisible infrastructure is always the one nobody thinks about until it fails

Sources:
1) Bill Dargue — A Brief History of Birmingham (Victorian & Medieval sections) — billdargue.jimdofree.com
2) Rapid Transition Alliance — The First Flush of Transition: The Rise of British Indoor Plumbing — rapidtransition.org
3) Elan Valley Official Site — History of the Elan Valley — elan-valley.co.uk
4) Born To Engineer — Engineering Marvel Turns 120: The Elan Valley Dams — borntoengineer.com

snippet.title: Why the Gin Craze Became One of England’s Worst Social Crises
snippet.description:
London in the 1700s faced one of the most shocking social crises in history—the Gin Craze. Cheap, unregulated alcohol flooded the streets, leading to widespread addiction, rising crime, and struggling families across the city. What started as a government-backed economic decision quickly spiraled into a public health disaster that affected thousands of lives.

In this video, we explore how gin became so dangerously popular, why it hit the poorest communities the hardest, and how London slowly pulled itself back from the edge. From the early rise of cheap distillation to the powerful impact of the Gin Act of 1751, this story reveals how policy, poverty, and human behavior collided in a way that changed history.

This video covers:
• The origins of the Gin Craze in 18th-century England
• Why gin became cheap and widely available
• The social impact—addiction, crime
• Failed government attempts to control consumption
• How the Gin Act of 1751 helped end the crisis

snippet.title: 1855: The Third Wave of Black Death – How 15 Million Vanished
snippet.description:
In 1855, the nightmare woke up. Emerging from the copper mines of Yunnan, China, the bubonic plague didn't just return—it evolved. This wasn't a slow-moving medieval sickness anymore; it was a modern traveler. It boarded steamships, rode first-class on global trade routes, and knocked on the doors of the world's most advanced cities, from Hong Kong to Bombay, and finally, to the streets of Glasgow and London.

This documentary uncovers the terrifying true story of the "Third Plague Pandemic," a 100-year catastrophe that claimed between 12 and 15 million lives. We dig into the forgotten history of how the Victorian era—obsessed with science and industry—came face-to-face with an ancient enemy they thought was extinct.

In this video, we uncover:

The Silent Voyage: How the plague hitched a ride on modern steamships to infiltrate every major port on Earth.

The Tale of Two Cities: The horrifying contrast between the brutal colonial response in British India and the "sanitized" panic in Europe.

The Glasgow Outbreak: The moment the Black Death struck a modern industrial city in Scotland.

The Suffolk Mystery: The bizarre and chilling story of how the plague hid in the English countryside for years without anyone noticing.

The Scientific War: How we finally identified the true killer (the rat flea) and the engineering feats that ended the pandemic.

snippet.title: 1500s York: The Medieval Megacity Where 50% of Life Was Survival
snippet.description:
In this history documentary, we strip away the romanticized "Merry Old England" myth to reveal what daily life was actually like in 16th-century York. From the claustrophobic, sunless tunnels of the Shambles to the open sewers running through the cobblestone streets, surviving in this walled Tudor city was not for the faint of heart.

But the dirt was only the beginning. You'll discover how York's fierce devotion to its Catholic roots put it on a deadly collision course with the most dangerous King in English history, leading to the devastating Pilgrimage of Grace uprising. We break down the brutal crackdowns, the terrifying executions of figures like Robert Aske and Margaret Clitherow, and how the city was forever changed by the Crown.

In this video, we cover:

Tudor Infrastructure: The genius (and squalor) of jettied houses and the crowded Ouse Bridge.

The Pilgrimage of Grace: How an army of 30,000 rebels turned York into a fortress against London.

The End of an Era: The suppression of the famous Mystery Plays and the rise of a secret, underground rebellion.

snippet.title: 1050: No Deodorant, No Modern Soap – Daily Life in Medieval England
snippet.description:
Imagine waking up in 1050 AD with no hot showers and no running water! Discover the surprising truth about daily life, hygiene, and how people actually stayed clean in 11th-century England.

Most movies show Medieval England as a filthy, mud-covered nightmare. But the reality of life in the 1000s and 1100s was remarkably different and highly resourceful! In this video, we explore the ingenious ways people took care of their personal hygiene without modern plumbing.

What This Video Covers:

The "Filthy" Stereotype: Why the idea of the completely unwashed medieval peasant is mostly a Hollywood myth.

Medieval Morning Routines: How they washed up daily using fresh well water and simple washbasins.

Natural Dental Care: The clever ways they kept their teeth clean using frayed hazel twigs and mint or wood ash.

The Bathroom Problem: How they managed castle garderobes and outdoor latrines.

Fresh Homes & Clean Clothes: How they used sweet-smelling rushes for their floors and tackled heavy linen laundry in the local rivers.

snippet.title: We Deciphered Ancient Text From 5000 Years Ago
snippet.description:
Irving Finkel lectures on Cuneiform, an ancient form of writing, dating all the way back to 5000 years ago. 

More than five thousand years ago, a revolutionary script emerged in the fertile lands of Mesopotamia that would transform how people counted, governed, worshipped and told stories. This was cuneiform, the world’s earliest known writing system.

In this episode of The Ancients, Tristan Hughes is joined by Dr Irving Finkel to uncover how cuneiform actually worked and how you would write it yourself. From humble beginnings as simple pictograms tracking beer and grain, to the wedge-shaped signs that recorded myths, laws and epic tales long before the Bible, this episode explores how cuneiform spread across Sumer, Babylon, Assyria and Persia — and why these clay tablets remain one of archaeology’s richest windows into the ancient world.

snippet.title: What was the Stone Age?
snippet.description:
The Stone Age was when people used stone tools, but that definition can be misleading. People didn't just use stone for tools, even though that is how the Stone Age is often depicted in popular culture. 

The Stone Age is called that because of all the materials people in the distant past used, stone is almost always the only thing that survives in an archeological site. Stone Age people in fact used a wide variety of materials, mostly organic.

An evil stepmother demands a maiden’s lungs and liver; a girl is ripped from a wolf’s stomach; and sisters mutilate their feet to squeeze into a gold slipper. During the early 1800s, brothers Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm gathered these unflinchingly gory details from stories circulating around what’s now Germany. Claudia Schwabe explores how these now-infamous tales evolved as they spread worldwide.

snippet.title: The Revolutionary War Was Bloodier Than You Think
snippet.description:
Forget what you learned in school. Or from Hamilton. The American revolution was bigger and bloodier than you ever thought.

For the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, we bring you the undiscovered stories, heroes, and villains of the War for Independence. In this incredible six-part retelling, we go far beyond the 13 original colonies and the clash between American Patriots and British colonial troops. We traverse the Atlantic and plunge deep into the American West to discover a multi-front war that engulfed a diverse cast of characters – Indigenous people, enslaved Africans, American Loyalists, women of all social classes – and changed the face of world history.

EPISODE 1: UNLIKELY REVOLUTIONARIES 
We begin by profiling three unlikely revolutionaries: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, and John Adams. 

EPISODE 2: REVOLUTION IN INDIAN COUNTRY 
When fighting breaks out between Britain and the American colonists, the native people of North America are forced to pick a side. 

EPISODE 3: THE SLAVES’ REVOLUTION
The American War for Independence was, in fact, two revolutions in one. There was the Revolution we know – of American Patriots against their British overlords. And there was the Revolution we don’t know – of enslaved Black people against their American overlords

Ingenious technologies built without modern machines

How medieval builders controlled heat, water, and airflow

Lost techniques that were efficient, sustainable, and durable

Why some of these ideas disappeared and why they’re being studied again today

Sometimes the past was smarter than we realize.

When we think about medieval kings and queens, our thoughts often conjure up images of glittering palaces. Of monarchs who are draped in ermine, velvet and dripping in jewels living a life of luxury. But behind the gleam of polished crowns and the pomp and ceremonial splendour, their world was anything but perfect. 

Because European royal families have a long, dark and twisted history of tangled genetics, with generations of intermarriage that they would prefer the royal record keepers kept buried. Let’s travel back and take a look at bricks and mortar, bloodlines and blind ambition.

snippet.title: The Most Revolutionary Ship Ever Built: Complete History of HMS Warrior
snippet.description:
In 1860, the world’s most powerful naval superpower faced a terrifying threat: a new generation of French ironclads. Britain’s response was the HMS Warrior, a ship so advanced it rendered every other warship on Earth obsolete overnight. Costing the equivalent of £1.5 billion ($1.9 billion) today, this "Black Snake" was the first armor-plated, iron-hulled battleship powered by a massive 4,000-horsepower steam engine—making it the fastest and most lethal predator on the high seas.

snippet.title: Let's Talk About Medieval Diseases...
snippet.description:
Support our non AI content from £3 on Patreon or YT Memberships for extra videos & bonus content, funded and influenced directly by you! https://www.patreon.com/cw/OfficialMedievalMadness

Just like people living today, the Medievals had a huge number of diseases doing the rounds. So, what illnesses did people face back then? Surprisingly, many of them are the same as ones we deal with today. The difference wasn’t the diseases themselves, it was the fact that the Medievals had no vaccinations, antibiotics, or modern medicines, so recovery often depended on rest, the strength of the patient’s own body and a whole lot of luck. Let’s travel back to the Middle Ages and take a look at medieval diseases, the ‘cures’ that did or in most cases didn’t work and ask the big question; did getting sick in the Middle Ages mean certain death?

snippet.title: The Hardest Etiquette Rules Women Had to Follow in Victorian London (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
They lived inside the most powerful empire on earth — and were given almost no power within it. This documentary explores the extraordinary world of women in 1800s England: the bizarre etiquette rules that governed their every move, the rigid daily routines they were expected to perform, the hobbies they were permitted, and the silent ways they pushed back against a system designed to keep them decorative and still. From the fan language of Victorian ballrooms to the women who crowded into a dark attic just to hear Parliament debate — this is the story of an era where even the angle of a skirt hem was written into a rule book.

What's covered in this documentary:
The Victorian social structure and class divide
The strangest etiquette rules from real period manuals
The calling card system and afternoon tea culture 
Women's hobbies and accomplishments

Sources: 
Cassell's Household Guide (1869)
Emily Thornwell, The Lady's Guide to Perfect Gentility (1856)
Florence Hartley, The Ladies' Book of Etiquette (1860)
Coventry Patmore, The Angel in the House (1854)
